extracted.intended_audience: researchers, librarians, publishers, and policymakers interested in academic open access and embargo policies
extracted.subtask_description: Describes policies and norms for embargoing access to academic journal content: definitions, types (moving wall, fixed date, current year), purposes (delayed OA, self-archiving, database access), typical durations, evidence about impacts, and exceptions (e.g., crises, Plan S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of embargo (academic publishing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An embargo is a period during which access to academic journals is not allowed to users who have not paid for access (or have access through their institution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to ensure publishers have revenue to support their activities; debate exists about whether embargoes actually affect publisher revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moving wall (type of embargo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'moving wall' is the time period between the last issue of an academic journal available in a given online database and the most recently published print issue; it is specified by publishers in their license agreements and generally ranges from several months to several years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by databases like JSTOR; implemented via license agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed date (type of embargo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fixed date is a particular time point that does not change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargoed content becomes available at a specific calendar date (as opposed to a moving-window scheme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Current year (type of embargo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A current year embargo sets a time point on Jan. 1 of the current year so that all material earlier than that is available; although fixed during the year, it changes each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for making all content published before the current year open while keeping the current year's content restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — delayed open access journals
rubrics_metrics.description: For delayed open access journals, the embargo separates the most recent period, for which a subscription is needed, from an older period, where a subscription is not needed and anyone may access the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embargo lengths for delayed OA can range from a few months to several years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — self-archiving embargo (copyright transfer agreements)
rubrics_metrics.description: For self-archiving, the embargo is a period set by the publisher in the copyright transfer agreement where access to the archived version of the article in a digital repository is restricted until the embargo expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical embargo periods range from 6 to 24 months, though some publishers may require up to 48 months; authors should check Sherpa/RoMEO and publisher agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — full-text databases embargoing recent content
rubrics_metrics.description: In full-text databases, an embargo separates the most recent period, where only a title or abstract is available, from an older period, which is openly accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include EBSCO and ProQuest; databases implement embargoes per publisher-specified terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical embargo durations by discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Currently used embargo times are often 6–12 months in STEM and over 12 months in social sciences and humanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These common practices are cited, but the article notes they do not seem to be based on robust empirical evidence about subscription impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability / evidence for embargo impact
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little empirical evidence that short or zero embargoes cause cancellation of subscriptions; 'there is no available evidence base to indicate that short or even zero embargoes cause cancellation of subscriptions' (UK House of Commons 2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data such as 'usage half life' exist but do not prove embargo length affects subscriptions; arguments that embargo protects subscription revenue are contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/exceptional lifting of embargoes (humanitarian crises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers have lifted embargo periods for specific research topics in times of humanitarian crises (e.g., outbreaks of Zika and Ebola), acknowledging that embargoes can stifle progress of science where timely information is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is cited as commendable and highlights tension between revenue protection and public-health/social benefits of immediate access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence evidence and Plan S zero-embargo principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence suggests traditional journals can peacefully coexist with zero-embargo self-archiving policies; Plan S includes zero-length embargoes on self-archiving as a key principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several studies and publisher examples are cited indicating no documented negative financial impact where zero embargoes are implemented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher practice examples and observed impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publishers (e.g., Royal Society, Sage, Emerald) have implemented zero embargo policies without documented financial impact; Highwire indicated society publishers make manuscripts freely available upon submission without apparent subscription decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete examples are offered as evidence against the necessity of embargo periods; authors and institutions can look to such publishers as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical perspective on value-added vs embargo rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: If the value publishers add beyond peer review (typesetting, dissemination, archiving) were worth the price, people might still pay even if an unformatted postprint is available elsewhere; an embargo can imply subscription prices are not commensurate with added value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an argument questioning publishers' justification for embargoes and supporting open-access/self-archiving advocacy.
